passages.title: Buffett 1987 Letter
passages.section: Mr. Market as a business partner
passages.text:
- He retells Ben Graham's allegory. Imagine market quotes coming from an emotional partner, Mr. Market, who offers every day to buy your share of a business or sell you his.
- Mr. Market's mood swings between euphoria (very high prices) and depression (very low prices), even when the underlying business is stable.
- You are free to ignore him; he will return tomorrow with a new price. The more erratic his moods, the better for the investor.
- The key warning: Mr. Market is there to serve you, not to guide you. His prices are useful; his opinions are not. If you cannot value your business better than he can, you should not be playing.
- Buffett says success comes from combining good business judgment with the ability to keep your thinking insulated from market emotion, not from formulas, computer models or price signals.
- He judges holdings by their operating results, not by daily or yearly quotes. He repeats Graham's idea that in the short run the market is a voting machine and in the long run a weighing machine. Slow recognition by the market can even help, because it allows buying more at bargain prices.

passages.title: Buffett 1987 Letter
passages.section: Other securities, portfolio insurance and the 1987 crash
passages.text:
- Berkshire's insurance float can go into five categories: long-term stocks, medium-term bonds, long-term bonds, cash equivalents and arbitrage. It picks whichever offers the best after-tax "mathematical expectation," but only among things it understands.
- He blames 1987's volatility on big money managers who focused on what other managers would do next, rather than on the businesses.
- He criticises "portfolio insurance," which mechanically sells more as prices fall — like selling pieces of a farm whenever a neighbour's land sells cheaper.
- His conclusion: volatile markets are good for real investors, small or large. Volatility can only hurt an investor who is forced, financially or psychologically, to sell at bad times.
- Berkshire found little to buy in stocks in 1987 but expected Mr. Market to offer chances later.

passages.title: Buffett 1993 Letter
passages.section: Why beta and volatility are the wrong measure of risk
passages.text:
- Academics define risk as a stock's volatility relative to the market (beta), calculated precisely from past prices. Buffett says this forgets that it is better to be approximately right than precisely wrong.
- For business owners this definition is absurd. Under beta theory, the Washington Post stock became "riskier" after it fell sharply in 1973. But the lower price made it a better deal, not a riskier one.
- True investors welcome volatility (Graham's Mr. Market again). Wild price swings mean solid businesses sometimes sell at irrationally low prices, and an investor free to ignore or exploit the market is not harmed by that.
- A beta purist studies only price history and ignores what the company makes, its competitors and its debt. Buffett prefers the opposite and would not mind if markets closed for a year or two after he bought.

passages.title: Buffett 1987 Letter
passages.section: Buying stocks as if buying a private business
passages.text:
- When Berkshire buys common stocks, it evaluates them as if buying part of a private business: the economic prospects, the people running it, and the price.
- It has no planned sale time or price. It will hold as long as intrinsic value keeps growing at a satisfactory rate.
- Buffett calls himself a business analyst — not a market analyst, a macroeconomic analyst or a security analyst.
- An active market is useful because it sometimes offers great prices, but it is not necessary. A long suspension of trading would not bother him.

reply:
Buffett uses "Mr. Market" as an allegory for the stock market.

Here's the core idea, based on the notes:

*   **Mr. Market is an emotional partner:** He constantly offers to buy or sell your shares, but his moods swing wildly between euphoria (very high prices) and depression (very low prices), even if the underlying business is stable.
*   **You should ignore his opinions:** Mr. Market is there to serve you, not guide you. You should not let his moods dictate your decisions.
*   **Volatility is an advantage:** The more erratic Mr. Market is, the better for the investor, provided you are not financially or psychologically forced to sell at bad times.
*   **Focus on fundamentals:** Success comes from combining good business judgment with the ability to keep your thinking insulated from market emotion, rather than relying on price signals or formulas.

In short, Mr. Market represents the unpredictable nature of market sentiment, and a good investor uses that randomness to find opportunities, while ignoring the noise.

passages.title: Buffett 1993 Letter
passages.text:
- Buffett and Munger decided long ago that it is too hard to make hundreds of smart decisions in a lifetime. Their strategy requires being smart only a few times; he says they will now settle for one good idea a year.
- Many experts would call this concentrated strategy riskier. Buffett disagrees. Concentration can *reduce* risk if it makes the investor think harder about a business and demand more comfort with its economics before buying.
- He defines risk using the dictionary: the possibility of loss or injury.

passages.title: Buffett 1993 Letter
passages.section: Knowing what you can't know; when diversification makes sense
passages.text:
- In many industries Buffett and Munger cannot tell a fad from a durable franchise, especially fast-changing technology businesses. They stick to easy cases.
- Wide diversification is right in two situations:
  - Strategies like arbitrage, where each bet carries real risk. Make many independent bets whose probability-weighted gains exceed their losses, like a casino that wants lots of small bets but refuses one huge bet.
  - An investor who does not understand business economics. They should buy a broad index fund in regular instalments, which will beat most professionals. When "know-nothing" money admits its limits, it stops being dumb.
- A "know-something" investor who can find five to ten sensibly priced companies with durable competitive advantages should not diversify conventionally. Putting money into a 20th-favourite idea instead of the best ones only lowers returns and raises risk.

passages.title: Marks 2006 Risk Memo
passages.section: Measuring risk before and after the fact
passages.text:
- Looking forward, risk is an opinion. There is no standard way to put a number on it, and rare "improbable disasters" make investments look safer than they are (he quotes Nassim Taleb on Russian roulette with a huge revolver).
- Looking back, risk still can't be measured. Something happening does not mean it was likely; something not happening does not mean it was unlikely.
- Taleb's "alternative histories": was a winner skilful or lucky? A weather forecaster's 70% chance of rain can't be judged from one day. Judging risk-adjusted performance takes skilled, subjective judgment, not precise volatility ratios.

passages.title: Nomad 2006 Annual Letter
passages.section: The equity yield curve: patience has value
passages.text:
- Sleep's "equity yield curve": in bonds, longer maturities pay more to compensate for risk. In stocks, he argues, business outcomes can be *more* predictable several years out than next quarter, so time can both raise and de-risk returns.
- He suggests academic economics has a blind spot here because it studies short time periods, while habits and brands (like Coca-Cola's) take decades to form.
- Evidence from Nomad's own portfolio: stocks held longest had the highest annualised returns, falling steadily for newer holdings — a gap of more than 10 percentage points a year. He admits survivorship and timing biases.
- Other investors held Nomad's stocks for about 20 weeks on average, while Nomad expected to hold for about 260 weeks. Most investors trade on reported numbers; Nomad focuses on the inputs that drive future value.

passages.title: Marks 2003 Most Important Thing
passages.section: The limits of macro forecasting; cycles; contrarianism
passages.text:
- Every investor must decide whether they belong to the "I know" school or the "I don't know" school. If you believe you can see the future, you concentrate and time the market. If not, you invest defensively and diversify. Marks is firmly in the second camp: survival comes first.
- Cycles are inevitable. Prices swing more than fundamentals, and extrapolating trends is one of the most dangerous things an investor can do.
- Contrarian behaviour works most reliably: only unpopular assets can be truly cheap. Distressed debt profits partly because no one loves a distressed company.
- Patient opportunism: Oaktree waits for sellers to call rather than chasing a buy list ("our investments find us"), and invests bottom-up.

passages.title: Marks 2003 Most Important Thing
passages.text:
- Above all, the relationship between price and value matters. No asset is so good it can't be a bad investment at too high a price, and few are so bad they can't be good investments if cheap enough.
- No asset class has a birthright to high returns. You'd ask the price before buying someone's car, so buying an investment without judging its price is just as silly. Examples: tech stocks in the late 1990s (bought at any price) and junk bonds in the 1970s-80s (avoided at any price).
- The biggest losses he has seen came from buying "perfect" companies at prices that assumed perfection. A good company is not the same as a good investment.
- He wants the best *buys*, not the best companies.

reply:
That's a common interpretation, but it's important to look at the actual notes.

Howard Marks doesn't necessarily say the *best time* to buy is always January. Instead, he focuses on **contrarian thinking and cycles** rather than specific calendar dates.

Here’s what the notes actually suggest about his approach:

*   **Cycles are Inevitable:** He emphasizes that prices swing more than fundamentals. This means waiting for market conditions that are *unpopular* or *distressed* (contrarian behavior) often leads to the best opportunities [S1].
*   **Value Over Price:** The key isn't the month; it’s the relationship between the price you pay and the actual value of the asset. He stresses buying a good business at a *reasonable* price, not just any price [S2].
*   **Patience:** His strategy is about waiting for "patient opportunism"—waiting for sellers to call rather than chasing a buy list [S1].

So, the takeaway isn't "Buy in January," but rather **"Be patient, be contrarian, and focus on buying businesses when the price reflects their true value."**
